query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor alloying addition of titanium (Ti) into the boride formulation will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, chemically inert TiB2‐rich interlayer during hot-dip aluminum plating. This interlayer will act as a barrier to molten aluminum, thus improving the component’s resistance to corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components fabricated by conventional methods exhibiting a typical boride microstructure without any deliberate secondary phase or dopant addition.
generation.intervention: Alloy the boride with a low level (approximately 2–5 wt%) of titanium during the component synthesis process.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at plating temperatures (approximately 650–700 °C) under standard hot-dip aluminum plating operational conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The titanium addition is expected to drive the nucleation and growth of a continuous, thin TiB2-rich interlayer along grain boundaries and at the surface during plating.
generation.mechanism: Titanium reacts with the boron in the matrix to form TiB2, which is both chemically inert and has a compatible lattice with the base boride. This ubiquitous TiB2 phase reduces the wetting and penetration of molten aluminum into the component and thereby lowers the kinetics of corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to unalloyed boride components, the Ti-alloyed variants will exhibit a reduced corrosion rate, observable as a lower corrosion depth and decreased weight loss after molten aluminum exposure (e.g., an anticipated improvement on the order of ~20%, though the precise value is uncertain).
generation.baseline: Standard boride-based components without titanium addition, which show a characteristic corrosion rate and interfacial degradation during molten aluminum exposure.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected under conventional hot-dip aluminum plating conditions (650–700 °C) and typical exposure durations. Its effectiveness may diminish if the exposure parameters (e.g., temperature significantly higher than 700 °C or unusually long immersion times) extend beyond the normal operational range.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement is uncertain; the optimal Ti content and long-term stability of the TiB2 interlayer under cyclic plating conditions require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of boride samples: one set with the Ti addition (2–5 wt%) and a control group without Ti. Subject both sets to identical molten aluminum immersion tests at ~660 °C for predetermined durations reflective of plating operations. Post-exposure, assess the corrosion depth, weight loss, and interfacial microstructure using SEM/EDS and XRD to verify the formation and continuity of the TiB2-rich layer.
measurements: Corrosion depth measured via cross-sectional microscopy (SEM).
Weight loss quantification before and after molten aluminum exposure.
Phase identification and continuity of the TiB2 interlayer using XRD and EDS mapping.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-alloyed samples do not consistently show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., less than ~15–20% improvement) in corrosion depth and weight loss relative to the baseline, or if no continuous TiB2 interlayer is observed, then the hypothesis should be rejected.
